era: Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt, 3rd century BC to 4th century AD
label: HISTORY
title: The Library of Alexandria: Did It Really Burn in a Single Day?
description: The Library of Alexandria is remembered as the greatest library of the ancient world, destroyed in one tragic fire. The real story is slower and stranger: confiscated books from ships, a catalogue of all knowledge, a purge of scholars, Caesar's fire, Aurelian's war and the end of the Serapeum. Here is how the library really disappeared.

lines.t: Jack, how do you picture the end of the Library of Alexandria?
A huge fire. Flames, scrolls burning, all the knowledge of the ancient world lost in one night.
That's the picture most people have. And according to most historians, that's not what happened.
So it didn't burn?
Parts of it may have burned, more than once. But the library seems to have faded away over several centuries, through politics, wars and neglect.
That's almost sadder.
It is. But to understand how it ended, we need to see how extraordinary it was at the start.
Who built it?
The idea may have come from Demetrius of Phalerum, an exiled Athenian statesman living in Alexandria. He may have proposed it to King Ptolemy the First, a former general of Alexander the Great.
But the library itself was probably built under his son, Ptolemy the Second, in the third century BC.
It was part of a larger research institution called the Mouseion, dedicated to the Muses, the nine goddesses of the arts. That's where our word museum comes from.
How many books did it have?
Nobody knows. Estimates range from forty thousand to seven hundred thousand scrolls. That huge range tells you how uncertain the numbers are.
Alexandria came to be regarded as the capital of knowledge and learning in the Greek world.
How did they collect so many books?
Aggressively. The Ptolemaic kings had well-funded policies for acquiring texts. They bought books at the book fairs of Rhodes and Athens.
And according to the Greek medical writer Galen, Ptolemy the Second decreed that any books found on ships arriving in the port should be taken to the library.
Confiscated?
Copied. Official scribes made copies. The library kept the original, and the owners received the copies.
The library was especially eager to collect manuscripts of Homer's poems, the foundation of Greek education.
Who worked there?
Some of the greatest minds of the ancient world. Zenodotus of Ephesus worked to standardise the texts of Homer.
Callimachus wrote the Pinakes, sometimes considered the world's first library catalogue.
Eratosthenes of Cyrene calculated the circumference of the Earth to within a few hundred kilometres.
Hero of Alexandria documented the first recorded steam engine. Aristophanes of Byzantium invented the system of accents used in written Greek.
So it wasn't just storage. It was a research centre.
Exactly. Under Ptolemy the Third, a second, daughter library was even founded in the Serapeum, a temple to the god Serapis.
When did things start to go wrong?
Long before any famous fire. In 145 BC, King Ptolemy the Eighth purged intellectuals from Alexandria.
The head librarian, Aristarchus of Samothrace, resigned and went into exile on Cyprus. Many other scholars fled to other cities, where they kept teaching.
So the knowledge spread out.
Yes. One historian of the time joked sarcastically that Alexandria had become the teacher of all Greeks and barbarians alike. Rival centres, like Pergamum, grew stronger.
From the middle of the second century BC, Ptolemaic rule in Egypt became less and less stable.
Now the famous fire.
In 48 BC, during his civil war, Julius Caesar was trapped in Alexandria. His forces set fire to ships in the harbour, and the fire spread.
The library, or part of its collection, burned. But it is unclear how much was destroyed. Ancient writers disagree.
Plutarch says the great library burned. Seneca quotes a lost work saying forty thousand scrolls were destroyed. Other writers say only ships and some houses near the sea burned.
And afterwards?
The institution seems to have survived, or been rebuilt soon after. The geographer Strabo visited the Mouseion around 20 BC, and scholars kept working there.
There's even a story, told by Plutarch, that Mark Antony gave Cleopatra two hundred thousand scrolls from the library of Pergamum. Plutarch himself warned that his source might be unreliable.
So when did it actually disappear?
The last known references to scholars belonging to the Mouseion date to the 260s AD.
In 272, Emperor Aurelian fought to recapture Alexandria from the forces of Queen Zenobia of Palmyra. His troops destroyed the Brucheion, the quarter where the main library stood.
And the daughter library in the Serapeum?
In 391, under the anti-pagan policies of Emperor Theodosius the First, the Serapeum was demolished on the orders of Bishop Theophilus of Alexandria.
Whether many books were still there by then is debated.
What about the story that the Arabs burned it?
Alexandria was taken by an Arab army in 642. Several Arabic sources written centuries later claim the caliph ordered the library destroyed. Historians generally treat that story as legend.
Is anything left today?
Almost nothing of the original library survives. But Alexandria has a new one.
The idea of reviving it was first proposed in 1974. UNESCO became involved, an international architecture competition was held in 1989, and the Norwegian firm Snøhetta won.
The Bibliotheca Alexandrina was completed in 2002. Today it is a modern library and cultural centre, commemorating the ancient one.
So, no single fire. Purges, civil wars, Caesar's flames, Aurelian's war, and the end of the Serapeum.
A library doesn't need to burn to disappear. It just needs to stop being cared for.
Which of these do you think did the most damage?
